subject: computer-science

moments.title: Moore's Law published
moments.body: In Electronics magazine, Moore (then at Fairchild Semiconductor) predicts the number of transistors per integrated circuit will double approximately every year. He revises to every two years in 1975. The prediction held for roughly 50 years before slowing in the 2010s.
moments.takeaway: A trend article in a trade magazine became the organising principle of an industry — partly because the industry organised to make it true.

moments.title: Intel 4004
moments.who: Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor, Masatoshi Shima, Intel
moments.body: The Intel 4004 ships in November 1971. It's the first commercially available microprocessor: a complete CPU on a single chip. 2,300 transistors, 740 kHz, designed for a Japanese calculator (the Busicom 141-PF). The deal terms allowed Intel to sell it for non-calculator uses.
moments.takeaway: The microprocessor was a calculator part. Its general-purpose use was a side-bet that became the entire industry.

now.title: Chips today
now.body: A 2024 high-end mobile SoC (Apple A18 Pro) has 20+ billion transistors at ~3nm. Moore's Law is widely declared dead but performance still scales (chiplets, 3D stacking, specialisation: GPUs, NPUs). TSMC fabricates the leading-edge chips for almost all major customers; the US CHIPS Act (2022) is a $52bn attempt to reshore manufacturing.
now.open_questions: How long can transistor scaling continue? Quantum effects, heat dissipation and lithography are all near physical limits.

reflection: Three of the 4004's designers were Italian, Japanese, Polish and American. Faggin (Italian-American) had to fight to get his name etched on the chip's mask. Silicon Valley has always been more international than its marketing suggests.
